questions.topic: The Workload-Driven Storage Decision Matrix
questions.question: Which set of workload axes drives storage service selection on GCP?
options: Team familiarity, console usability, SLA tier, and regional availability of the product
Programming language, framework support, SDK maturity, and client library coverage
Structure, access pattern, scale, latency, and consistency/distribution requirements
Encryption options, IAM integration, audit logging depth, and compliance certifications

questions.topic: The Workload-Driven Storage Decision Matrix
questions.question: What most fundamentally distinguishes an OLTP workload from an OLAP workload?
options: Many small transactional point reads and writes by key versus large scans and aggregations over many rows
Structured relational data with joins versus semi-structured documents with flexible nested schemas
Single-region deployments with zonal failover versus multi-region deployments with consensus replication
Data that fits on one machine versus data that must be sharded horizontally across many machines

questions.topic: The Workload-Driven Storage Decision Matrix
questions.question: An IoT platform ingests 500,000 sensor readings per second, serves the latest reading per device in under 10 ms, and supports daily analyst aggregates. What does the decision matrix output?
options: Cloud SQL for the writes with read replicas dedicated to serving the analyst aggregation queries
Firestore for device documents, since its real-time listeners can push the latest readings instantly
BigQuery alone, since it handles both the streaming ingestion and the analytical aggregations
Bigtable for ingestion and low-latency serving, with a pipeline feeding BigQuery for analytics

questions.topic: The Workload-Driven Storage Decision Matrix
questions.question: A team runs heavy analytical reporting queries directly against the Cloud SQL primary that also serves their checkout flow. What failure mode does the decision matrix predict?
options: The reporting queries return stale results because Cloud SQL replicas are eventually consistent
The analytical scans saturate the primary and degrade latency for the transactional traffic
The reporting queries fail outright because Cloud SQL cannot execute large aggregations
The database silently drops rows under load because OLTP engines shed excess read traffic

questions.topic: The Workload-Driven Storage Decision Matrix
questions.question: A startup's 10 GB regional app database runs fine on Cloud SQL, but an architect proposes Spanner "so we never have to migrate." What is the strongest objection grounded in workload-driven selection?
options: Spanner cannot enforce relational constraints, so the schema would lose its integrity guarantees
Spanner only supports eventually consistent reads, which the checkout workload cannot tolerate
Spanner requires denormalizing the schema into documents before any migration can proceed
Spanner carries a cost floor for distributed capacity the workload has shown no need for

questions.topic: The Workload-Driven Storage Decision Matrix
questions.question: A single workload needs transactional writes by key at high volume and also large historical aggregations. Which response reflects expert use of the decision matrix?
options: Pick one service that scores acceptably on both halves so the architecture stays simple
Reject the requirements as contradictory until the product team drops one of the two halves
Split the workload across a transactional store and an analytical copy connected by a pipeline
Choose the most general product available so future requirements are covered in advance

questions.topic: Relational Options: Cloud SQL vs AlloyDB vs Spanner
questions.question: How does Cloud SQL scale write throughput?
options: Vertically only, by moving the single primary instance to a larger machine
Horizontally, by adding write-capable nodes that share a distributed log
Automatically, by splitting hot tables across replicas as load increases
Elastically, by queueing writes in a buffer tier during traffic spikes

questions.topic: Relational Options: Cloud SQL vs AlloyDB vs Spanner
questions.question: What role does TrueTime play in Spanner?
options: It schedules maintenance windows so replicas across regions never restart at the same moment
It measures replication lag between regions so reads can be routed to the freshest replica
It synchronizes backup snapshots across regions so restores are consistent to the second
It bounds clock uncertainty so transaction timestamps can guarantee external consistency

questions.topic: Relational Options: Cloud SQL vs AlloyDB vs Spanner
questions.question: A Postgres application needs faster transactional throughput than Cloud SQL delivers plus real-time analytical reads on operational data, all within one region. Which service fits best?
options: Spanner, because its horizontal write scaling covers any throughput requirement
Cloud SQL with more read replicas, because replicas absorb the analytical scans
AlloyDB, because its disaggregated storage and columnar engine serve hybrid workloads
Bigtable, because its linear node scaling handles both transactions and analytics

questions.topic: Relational Options: Cloud SQL vs AlloyDB vs Spanner
questions.question: A payments ledger must accept concurrent writes from the EU and US and survive a full regional outage with zero data loss. Why is Cloud SQL with HA insufficient?
options: Its HA configuration fails over to a standby in another zone, which does not survive a regional outage
Its storage engine cannot hold financial data because it lacks ACID transaction support
Its read replicas would serve stale balances, violating the ledger's consistency requirement
Its backup schedule runs daily, so up to a day of committed transactions would be lost

questions.topic: Relational Options: Cloud SQL vs AlloyDB vs Spanner
questions.question: A Spanner table uses a commit-timestamp column as the leading primary key component, and one server is saturated while others idle. What explains this?
options: TrueTime uncertainty intervals force all timestamped writes through a single coordinator node
Sequentially increasing keys funnel every insert to the last split, hotspotting one server
Paxos consensus requires a fixed leader replica to sequence all writes for the whole table
The table has too few secondary indexes, so lookups scan the same split repeatedly

questions.topic: Relational Options: Cloud SQL vs AlloyDB vs Spanner
questions.question: On the exam, which combination of requirements is the reliable signal that Spanner is the intended answer rather than Cloud SQL or AlloyDB?
options: Relational schema together with global distribution and strongly consistent writes
Relational schema together with high availability and automated daily backups
Relational schema together with analytical reads and sub-second dashboard queries
Relational schema together with Postgres compatibility and minimal migration effort

questions.topic: NoSQL Options: Firestore vs Bigtable vs Memorystore
questions.question: Why is row key design the central schema decision in Bigtable?
options: Because rows are sorted by key and there are no secondary indexes, the key defines every efficient access path
Because keys determine which column families a row may contain, constraining the data model up front
Because keys are hashed across nodes randomly, so poor keys break the even distribution of storage
Because keys are immutable after creation, so mistakes require dropping and reloading the table

questions.topic: NoSQL Options: Firestore vs Bigtable vs Memorystore
questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts Firestore's consistency with Bigtable's replication?
options: Firestore reads are eventually consistent, while Bigtable replication is strongly consistent
Both offer strong consistency everywhere, differing only in latency and pricing model
Firestore reads are strongly consistent, while Bigtable cross-cluster replication is eventually consistent
Both are eventually consistent, differing only in how quickly replicas converge

questions.topic: NoSQL Options: Firestore vs Bigtable vs Memorystore
questions.question: A recommender needs per-user feature vectors fetched by user ID in single-digit milliseconds across billions of users. Which store is the design-center match?
options: Firestore, because document reads are strongly consistent and automatically indexed
Bigtable, because key-addressed reads stay low latency at petabyte scale
Memorystore, because feature lookups belong in RAM for the fastest reads
Cloud SQL, because feature vectors are structured rows suited to a relational table

questions.topic: NoSQL Options: Firestore vs Bigtable vs Memorystore
questions.question: A team stores session state and rate-limit counters in Memorystore without snapshots enabled. After a maintenance restart the data is gone and users are logged out. What was the design error?
options: Choosing Redis structures like sorted sets, which are not preserved across restarts
Skipping read replicas, which are required for Memorystore data to survive failover
Treating an in-memory cache tier as a system of record for state that must persist
Disabling eviction policies, which caused the instance to clear itself under pressure

questions.topic: NoSQL Options: Firestore vs Bigtable vs Memorystore
questions.question: An analytics job runs a daily query that returns 10 million small Firestore documents for aggregation, and the bill spikes. What is the root cause?
options: Firestore bills per document read, so scan-heavy analytical access multiplies costs
Firestore composite indexes rebuild on every query, doubling the read throughput
Firestore real-time listeners re-deliver each document to the job as it changes
Firestore transactions lock each document read, forcing retries that bill again

questions.topic: NoSQL Options: Firestore vs Bigtable vs Memorystore
questions.question: A Bigtable table for sensor telemetry uses row keys beginning with the event timestamp. Writes overwhelm one tablet server while the rest sit idle. Which redesign fixes it?
options: Add composite indexes on the timestamp column so lookups spread across the cluster
Lead the key with a device or entity identifier so writes distribute across the keyspace
Increase the cluster's node count so the hot tablet is rebalanced onto new servers
Move recent data to Memorystore so the hot tablet only handles historical reads

questions.topic: GCS Storage Classes and Lifecycle Management
questions.question: What actually differs between GCS storage classes?
options: Durability guarantees, which drop as the storage price per gigabyte decreases
Storage price versus retrieval fees and minimum durations, at identical durability
Replication topology, since colder classes keep only a single copy of each object
Access latency, since colder classes take hours to return the first byte

questions.topic: GCS Storage Classes and Lifecycle Management
questions.question: What is the minimum storage duration for each non-Standard GCS class?
options: Nearline 60 days, Coldline 180 days, and Archive 365 days
Nearline 7 days, Coldline 30 days, and Archive 90 days
Nearline 30 days, Coldline 90 days, and Archive 365 days
Nearline 30 days, Coldline 60 days, and Archive 180 days

questions.topic: GCS Storage Classes and Lifecycle Management
questions.question: A 10 TB embeddings snapshot in Nearline is fully re-read every month for reprocessing. Compared with Standard, what is the economic outcome?
options: The savings roughly double because Nearline discounts both storage and reads
The retrieval fees roughly cancel the storage savings, so nothing is gained
The costs rise sharply because Nearline charges a fee per object listed
The savings hold because retrieval fees only apply to cross-region reads

questions.topic: GCS Storage Classes and Lifecycle Management
questions.question: A lifecycle rule moves objects to Coldline at age 30 days, but a cleanup script deletes many of those objects at age 40 days. What billing consequence follows?
options: Early-deletion charges apply, billing each object as if it had stayed the full 90 days
No consequence follows, since deletion is free once objects leave Standard class
Retrieval fees apply retroactively to every read the object served while in Coldline
The rule reverts the objects to Standard first, incurring a class-transition penalty

questions.topic: GCS Storage Classes and Lifecycle Management
questions.question: A bucket holds mixed data whose future access patterns nobody can predict, and per-prefix lifecycle rules are sprawling. Which approach fits best?
options: Enable Autoclass so the bucket moves objects between classes based on observed access
Default everything to Archive since it is cheapest and durability is identical anyway
Split the bucket per team and let each team hand-tune its own transition rules
Keep everything in Standard permanently since misclassification risk outweighs savings

questions.topic: GCS Storage Classes and Lifecycle Management
questions.question: Which misclassification is the expensive one to make, and why?
options: Cold data left in Standard, because idle objects incur retrieval fees while unused
Hot data placed in Archive, because frequent reads pay the highest retrieval fees
Cold data placed in Coldline, because transitions between cold classes are billed
Hot data left in Standard, because Standard carries the largest per-read charges

questions.topic: Migration Services: Datastream, DMS, BigQuery Data Transfer, Transfer Appliance
questions.question: What is the core distinction between DMS and Datastream?
options: DMS migrates a database toward cutover and retirement of the source, while Datastream continuously replicates changes for analytics
DMS handles NoSQL sources exclusively, while Datastream handles relational sources exclusively for its replication work
DMS moves data over the network, while Datastream requires shipping a physical appliance for its initial load
DMS only copies schemas and metadata, while Datastream copies the actual row data continuously

questions.topic: Migration Services: Datastream, DMS, BigQuery Data Transfer, Transfer Appliance
questions.question: How does Datastream capture changes from a source database?
options: By polling tables on a schedule with SELECT queries filtered on updated-at columns
By installing triggers on every table that write change rows into a staging table
By tailing the database transaction log, such as the MySQL binlog or Postgres WAL
By snapshotting the full database hourly and computing row-level diffs between snapshots

questions.topic: Migration Services: Datastream, DMS, BigQuery Data Transfer, Transfer Appliance
questions.question: A team schedules daily loads from Google Ads and an Amazon S3 bucket into BigQuery and wants zero pipeline code. Which service is the intended fit?
options: Datastream, since it streams source changes continuously into BigQuery tables
BigQuery Data Transfer Service, since it runs declarative scheduled loads into BigQuery
Storage Transfer Service, since it moves objects between clouds on a schedule
Database Migration Service, since it handles ongoing replication from external sources

questions.topic: Migration Services: Datastream, DMS, BigQuery Data Transfer, Transfer Appliance
questions.question: An analytics copy is built by polling source tables with SELECT queries every 15 minutes. Compared with log-based CDC, which defect is inherent to this design?
options: The polling approach cannot preserve column types, so numeric precision degrades in the copy
The polling approach doubles storage costs because each poll writes a full new snapshot
The polling approach requires stopping the source database briefly during every cycle
The polling approach misses deleted rows entirely and adds repeated query load to the source

questions.topic: Migration Services: Datastream, DMS, BigQuery Data Transfer, Transfer Appliance
questions.question: A company must move 1 PB from an on-premises datacenter that has a dedicated 1 Gbps uplink. Roughly how long would a saturated network transfer take, and what does that imply?
options: About 9 days, so an online transfer is clearly preferable to shipping hardware
About 90 days, so Transfer Appliance wins despite its shipping round-trip time
About 9 hours, so Storage Transfer Service handles it within a single window
About 900 days, so the dataset must be reduced before any move is feasible

questions.topic: Migration Services: Datastream, DMS, BigQuery Data Transfer, Transfer Appliance
questions.question: A retailer wants its Cloud SQL orders data queryable in BigQuery with freshness of a few minutes, without adding query load to the primary. Which design meets all three constraints?
options: DMS replication into a BigQuery dataset with a cutover scheduled once lag reaches zero
BigQuery Data Transfer Service pulling from Cloud SQL exports staged hourly in GCS
Datastream reading the transaction log and streaming change events into BigQuery
A read replica in Cloud SQL that analysts query directly instead of BigQuery
